messages.subject_clean: colonization and extinction both increase with increasing values of a covariate
messages.body_plain:
We are using colext for multi-season occupancy modeling for point count observations of birds.

To visualize some of our results for one of the species, we have graphed predicted values of a Vegetation Variable Y (specifically, basal area of two tree species at each point) against gamma and epsilon separately for each year (the parameter estimate for this variable is significant in both gamma and epsilon models).

What I notice is that the probability of both colonization AND extinction increase across the same range of the vegetation variable (basal area of two tree species) in at least some of the same years. This seems biologically odd to me, if I am understanding correctly, as we would interpret these results as "If a site is unoccupied, the probability of it being colonized increases with increasing  basal area" but also "If this site is occupied, the probability of it becoming unoccupied increases with increasing basal area." It would make more sense biologically to me if one probability was positively associate with the veg variable and the other were negatively related (or not related at all).

Is there any reason to think that this points to something wrong in our analysis?

Some background: Because there were multiple best models (delta AIC < 2), we used model-averaging to calculate predicted values. To get predicted values of gamma and epsilon for a given variable, we calculated values across the range of observed values for that variable, while other variables were assigned their mean observed value.

Thanks for any thoughts on this....

Sharon

messages.subject: Re: Zero-inflation and overdispersion in pcountOpen
messages.body_plain:
Hi Giancarlo,

I would be curious to hear more about the distribution of your counts on two levels. First, what is the distribution of your counts across sites and secondly what is your distribution of counts within sites? Also, how many sites to you have? Open abundance models like those implemented in pcountOpen tend to require a very large number of sites for convergence. Adding in challenges of zero inflation and overdispersion might make fitting your data in pcountOpen difficult. I have had more success with these models using the autoreg option in dynamics. In terms of your original question, I think seeing a distribution of counts by site in the form of histograms would be helpful for determining if the data are likely to fit a ZIP model (i.e. within sites does it look Poisson distributed other than the zeros). Either way it's difficult to know when the data will fit a particular distribution because the distributions are after the covariates are accounted for (lambda is Poisson distributed and lambda = exp(a + b1*x1 + ... + bn*xn).

I am a bit skeptical about the idea of using y/5 and then multiplying estimates by 5. One problem would be that any counts not evenly divisible by 5 would not be integers and a Poisson distribution expects integers.

Ideally you would have covariates that could explain any extra Poisson variation on the upper end of the distribution and a zero-inflation factor to account for extra zeros. Then you could use a ZIP model without a problem. I have found that negative binomial models generate biologically unrealistic estimates, particularly in the upper 95% CI estimates of N[i]. It could be better to use an imperfect ZIP model than an unrealistic but good fitting ZINB model when you have large mean non-zero counts.

Sorry, that get's rather far afield of your original question but hopefully it gives you some things to try over the weekend.
Cheers,
Dan

Hi Dan, thanks for taking the time to consider my flawed logic and for your helpful perspectives.

This data is from 42 years of lek counts (1 count/lek/year) of a prairie grouse at 255 leks.  I've trimmed the set to 88 leks having >= 10 counts and >= 30 years between the first and last surveys per lek.  Counts are highly dynamic and are confounded by local population health/habitat and detection issues (to which we can all relate!). I'm primarily interested in overall estimates of recruitment and survival and, currently, have no other site covariates other than the obvious site-year and/or detection covariate of count year.

I've made some .png files and some descriptive stats of distributions

All data: http://wp.me/a31SIX-3C
1,802 counts, 990 (55%) zeros, mean = 4.7, variance = 45.4, max = 40.

Across-lek summary: http://wp.me/a31SIX-3B
1. A mean 58% (SE = 3%) of counts within leks were zero counts.
2. The mean mean count was 4.3 (SE = 0.4) (includes zeros)
3. The mean max count was 15.5 (SE = 0.8).  17 leks had a max count over 20, five leks had a max count over 30.
4. The mean # of counts within sites was 20.5 (SE = 0.7)

So, to the last point, I haven't found previous discussion of missing data (which is about 50% in this data set) in running Dail-Madsen / pcountOpen models. I know some of the other unmarked-implemented models (e.g. colext) are flexible about missing data and I'd be very interested to hear from anyone (Richard?) about any issues associated with with missing observations in pcountOpen.

I have been experimenting with the different distributions (and different K values) using the autoregressive dynamic and an intercept-only model and have found the NB distribution to have a far lower AIC than P or ZIP models (ZIP models being nearly 2 AIC > than P models).  Perhaps the extra zeros aren't an issue here or are being accounted for in the detection component of the model (?).  I've been upping the K from 50 to 100 to 200 (with ever-increasing calculation times) and estimates continue to improve.  Parameter estimates, predictions (just linear combs at this point), and BUPs look reasonable.  This is as far as I've gone with this, mostly due to the time required when K = 200+.  I hope to eventually include year-specific detection, recruitment and/or survival.

Thanks again, Dan, and all else who offer insight/suggestions here.

Giancarlo

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Model validation
messages.body_plain:
In the past I have built a detection function and then saw how many validation sites had "adequate" sampling given the amount of times we had searched there.  e.g., if you have a per-visit p of 0.25, to get a >90% chance that you did not miss the animal, you'd need to go at least 9 times:

1-(1-p)^#searches = prob of at least 1 detection given the total # of searches

Then if I had sampled this minimum number of times to get over some threshold total probability (such as 85, 90 or 95%, whatever you think is good enough), I'd be confident in counting the 0's as true 0's.  Some of your non-detection sites will not beat this threshold and you will have to discard them for validation, especially if you have a detection model with covariates where this "cumulative" probability of detection might be pretty low...which will also tell you something about how much you ought to sample in certain places in the future. You then have a set of presences and "confident" absences with which to find kappa or AUC, etc.

Generally, raster based proportions have to be converted into predicted 0's or 1's.  Most people traditionally just go with >0.5 = 1; <0.5 = 0, but there are some techniques to find an "optimized" presence/absence threshold based on maximizing sensitivity and/or specificity or maintaining the original species prevalence.  See Freeman and Moisen's paper for a very good summary:
http://www.fs.fed.us/rm/pubs_other/rmrs_2008_freeman_e002.pdf

They also wrote an R package that can do most habitat suitability modeling/validation stuff for you once you have your predictions and a set of (independent) validation data.

Chris

Before collecting the data I marked out a fixed radius using flagging tape so the area of each point count is known. messages.body_plain:
Hi Jorge,

the GOF test for colext in our vignette is wrong: it always indicates a fitting model. We will correct this.

It is my understanding that no GOF test can be conducted directly for a binary response. The deviance and other measures of fit are uninformative about fit in the case of a binary response (this can be read somewhere in the GLM bible by McCullagh & Nelder for instance). One has to aggregate the response in some way before the usual GOF techniques can be applied.

What I did in the context of a dynamic occupancy model fitted in BUGS to binary data with three secondary reps was to aggregate the data to detection frequencies and conducted a Bayesian posterior predictive check of GOF to this binomial variant of the response, based on a chisquare discrepancy. (Note that I still fitted the model to the binary response though.) This indicated my model did not fit; hence, that appeared like an improvement ;)

I hope that something similar can be done for a likelihood analysis in unmarked. We have to check this out.

Kind regards  ----- Marc

I think I was trying to say that gdistsamp() will not directly estimate a trend parameter. But it can be used to abundance at various points in time. The thing to remember is that the model for abundance (N) is:

Dear Eric,

thank you for remining me that in „my own“ vignette, there is a counter example to my claim that the GOF test we give there does not work ... To be honest, I had forgotten this. In a couple of other examples with simulated data for a binary response, the test failed to indicate a non-fitting model. I don’t understand why it does show lack of fit in our example, because from my reading of the literature (for instance some parts in McCullagh and Nelder), we can’t do any GOF test directly for a binary response, but we always have to aggregate the response first. I will check this in our case and report back sometime.

Couple of more remarks:

(1)                GOF for binary response: the key thing to me seems to be whether your response is strictly binary (i.e., only 0 or 1) or whether it is some aggregation of binary numbers. If you have counts with values other than strictly zeroes and ones, then Chisquare and similar GOF tests should be OK. In the Island jay paper (Sillett et al. 2012), the response was a vector containing the counts of birds observed per distance class, and so this should be OK with our test. If you have a logistic regression (i.e., binomial GLM) with non-binary data (i.e., where the sample size or binomial index, N, is greater than 1 for some or most responses), then the test should also be OK, because then you have naturally „aggregated“ data (remember the binomial is the sum of N Bernoullis). However, it is my understanding that with binary responses, no discrepancy measure can be directly used to inform about lack of fit.

(2)                Residuals: residuals have an important place in model criticism also in GLMs, and I like to think about the hierarchical models that we fit using unmarked (or BUGS, JAGS etc) as 2 or more nested GLMs. So of course, there should be a way how we can compute residuals and inspect them to see whether they truly look like a starry sky or whether there is some remaining structure perhaps related to some covariates. I don’t have much experience in this in the context of GLMs, but I have long thought that I should explore residual checking in these HMs much more.

(3)                Quantifying the magnitude of lack of fit: Let’s assume you fit a hierarchial GLM with a reponse other than binary and do a parametric boostrap GOF test using some discrepancy measure such as Chisquare. Then, rather than using the parametric boostrap GOF to simply give you a “yes-no“ answer to the question of whether the model fits, it may be more interesting to give you an indication of how far your model is from a model that fits. I think that one could perhaps compute some „lack of fit statistic“ by dividing the GOF measure for your model by that of a perfectly fitting model (which would be the mean of the bootstrap distribution). ---- In the capture-recapture literature (e.g., CJS model), people have long quantified the lack of fit of a model using a c-hat statistics and often inflate their SEs by the square root of that to account for „overdispersion“ (assuming that all lack of fit is some sort of unstructured noise rather due to a structural failure of the model). It appears to me that if this is a sensible thing to do for CJS models, then perhaps something like that could be done in the kinds of HMs we fit in unmarked as well ?

Kind regards  ----  Marc
